strengths: MP-Bench is a genuinely large-scale and well-motivated resource: 421,363 pairs of hourly ERA5 fields (5 variables x 37 pressure levels) paired with official CMA warnings, aligned on a 12-hour window anchored at warning issuance time rather than using temporal averaging. The breadth (7 severe weather types, nationwide coverage, ~2,400 stations) clearly exceeds prior datasets such as WeatherQA (8,000 events) or CLLMate (41,000 events).

The paper defines four distinct QA task types (MC, T/F, RSW, NSW) spanning different spatial granularities and output formats, which increases the benchmark's usefulness for diagnosing MLLM capabilities beyond simple classification.

The proposed modules (DTGF temporal gating, TGS text-driven spatial masking, TGCA text-driven channel attention) are conceptually sensible for 4D meteorological data and avoid the common practice of compressing fields to RGB images or daily averages. The ablation study over all eight module combinations (Table 3) supports that each module contributes, and the full combination is best.

Evaluation is reasonably broad: four open-source MLLMs plus GPT-4o, per-weather-type analysis (Fig. 5), and interpretability analysis of module weights (Figs. 6, 8, 9) that are qualitatively consistent with physical expectations (e.g., higher temporal weights for severe vs. normal weather).

The appendix provides substantial reproducibility detail: complete prompt templates for all four QA types, the GPT-4o scoring rubric, dataset statistics by year/type/month, and full LLaMA-Factory training/evaluation hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Fundamental concern about problem framing / label validity: the model is given ERA5 reanalysis fields for the 12 hours [t, t+11] starting at warning issuance time t. Warnings state that severe weather is 'expected to occur... within the next few hours,' so the input reanalysis window contains the actual observed event the model is asked to 'predict.' This makes the task closer to postdiction/explanation than to the operational forecasting the paper claims (an 'AI weather station' issuing rolling warnings). This weakens the central contribution claim and is not acknowledged or discussed in the manuscript.

The TGS and TGCA formulations contain technical inconsistencies: Eq. (5) defines G(u,v) using (u_j, v_j) but the index is over i = 1..N_coord; Eq. (6) sums G_j(u_i, v_i) with indices swapped relative to the stated definitions and conflates N_coord and N_ERA5; Eq. (9) for TGCA has ambiguous dimensional structure (v P^T P). The DTGF gate g_t = sigma(MLP(||x_t - x_{t-1}||_2)) collapses each timestep to a scalar norm, which appears to discard most of the spatial/channel information the module is claimed to exploit. These errors undermine confidence in the reported implementations.

Baseline design is weak and possibly misleading. Table 2 reports all open-source models already enhanced with the three modules, so the reader cannot cleanly separate the value of the raw MLLM from the added modules without cross-referencing the 5,000-sample ablation (Table 3). The GPT-4o comparison uses only 4 variables compressed into 3 channels — a strawman setup that largely explains its near-zero scores and does not represent what a well-engineered GPT-4o pipeline could achieve.

Absolute performance is modest and the headline gains are partially a consequence of severe class imbalance: gale (40%+) and normal (~12%) dominate while snow storm is ~1.5-1.7% and achieves <6% accuracy. Accuracy on imbalanced classes overstates practical utility; no balanced metrics (per-class F1, precision/recall) are reported. NSW generative scores remain extremely low (2.1/5), suggesting the model does not actually perform the most practically valuable task well.

Ablation results are internally inconsistent with the narrative: DTGF alone reduces T/F accuracy (57.23 vs. 58.47 baseline) and several module combinations degrade MC-sub relative to their single-module variants; the claimed '36.01% overall gain' is a relative percentage that obscures modest absolute differences. No statistical significance or variance across seeds is reported.

Several presentation issues reduce clarity: module naming is inconsistent (TGF/DTGF), there are duplicated typo phrases ('RSW Questions and RSW Questions'), misspellings ('girdded', 'griddid'), and the description of the MC task says 'four options' while the template shows ~26 options. The test set is described only as 'a subset of 2024 data' without specifying size or sampling, which limits reproducibility of the headline numbers.

The claimed novelty ('first time MLLM has been used to deeply interpret raw meteorological data and generate warning conclusions') is overstated given closely related multimodal weather MLLM datasets/models (WeatherQA, CLLMate, ClimateIQA) discussed in the paper itself, and the restriction to China plus ERA5 reanalysis (rather than real-time NWP output) limits the claimed path to operational deployment.
Code and dataset are only promised, not yet released, so the contribution cannot currently be verified or used by the community.

strengths: MP-Bench is a substantial data contribution: 421,363 pairs aligning hourly ERA5 reanalysis (5 variables, 37 pressure levels, full 4D structure) with CMA severe weather warnings, covering seven event types across China — larger and temporally finer than prior multimodal weather benchmarks (SEVIR, WeatherQA, CLLMate, OmniEarth-Bench).

The QA suite spans four task granularities (MC, T/F, RSW, NSW), providing a reusable evaluation surface for meteorological MLLMs, and the appendix documents prompts, data statistics, and GPT-4o scoring rubrics in reasonable detail.

The three proposed modules (DTGF temporal gating, TGS text-driven Gaussian spatial masking, TGCA text-conditioned channel attention) are simple, plausible, and accompanied by an ablation showing each contributes, plus qualitative weight visualizations that connect to meteorological intuition (e.g., 950 hPa humidity sensitivity).
weaknesses: Fundamental task-definition concern: the model ingests ERA5 reanalysis over the 12-hour window (t to t+11) aligned with the warning issuance time. Because ERA5 is a reanalysis product describing the atmosphere during the warning window, the model is largely classifying concurrent/near-past conditions rather than 'predicting' future severe weather. The paper's framing as an end-to-end severe weather *prediction* system is therefore overstated; no true lead-time forecast protocol (input strictly before warning issuance, verified against subsequent observations) is evaluated.

The closed-source comparison (GPT-4o) is not fair or informative: GPT-4o receives heavily degraded, synthetically RGB-ified 3-channel u/v/total-precipitation inputs, while the proposed MMLM receives the full 185-channel 4D data. The ~35-60 point gaps in Table 2 mostly reflect this asymmetric input compression, not model capability.

Missing the most important baseline: no conventional classifier (e.g., a CNN/transformer trained directly on ERA5 for event classification) is compared. Without this, the paper cannot establish that the LLM/MLLM machinery adds value over standard supervised learning on the same data — a central claim for an 'AI weather warning' paper.

Evaluation inconsistencies and weak rigor: Table 2 reports MC-main 72.37 for the full model, while the ablation (Table 3) tops out at 57.23 even for the full configuration, with the discrepancy explained only vaguely by a 5,000-sample resampling; several ablation rows are non-monotonic (e.g., T/F degrades with DTGF alone vs. baseline); no significance tests or confidence intervals; the NSW task has only 651 samples and scores near 2%, and NSW scoring relies entirely on GPT-4o-as-judge without human verification.

Train/test split is confusing and possibly inconsistent: the text says 2023 for training and a 2024 subset for testing, yet Figure 4's caption says '(2023)'. With only two years of data, both train and test are dominated by a single annual cycle, and the test year's distribution (documented in the appendix) differs substantially, raising distribution-shift and data-leakage questions that are not analyzed.

Snow storm accuracy is ≤6% for all models (only ~1.7% of data), yet the paper still draws broad conclusions about 'unified spatiotemporal reasoning capability' from Fig. 5 without addressing class imbalance mitigation or per-class calibration.

Novelty claims are not carefully positioned: the claim of being 'the first' to use an MLLM to deeply interpret raw meteorological data and generate sentence-form warnings is undercut by the paper's own related work (WeatherQA, CLLMate, ExMVLM, OmniEarth-Bench), and the modules are straightforward applications of gating, Gaussian masking, and cross-attention rather than a methodological advance.

Presentation quality issues: module naming is inconsistent (Dynamic Temporal Gating Fusion vs. Dynamic Time-Gated Fusion); Figure 4 caption contradicts the split description; duplicate table numbering between main text and appendix; typos (e.g., 'MLLsfrom'); Figure 2 shows t+12 for a 12-hour window spanning t to t+11.

Reproducibility is promised but not yet delivered ('will be made publicly available'), and key details (test-set composition, exact GPT-4o judging protocol for RSW/NSW, how 'normal' negatives were sampled and matched) are underspecified.

strengths: Substantial and novel dataset contribution: MP-Bench provides 421,363 pairs of 4D ERA5 data (5 variables, 37 pressure levels, 12-hour windows) aligned with official CMA severe weather warnings — Table 1 shows no existing dataset concurrently offers large-scale textual warnings with comprehensive 4D meteorological coverage across 7 event types, making this a clear gap-filling resource for the community.

Well-designed benchmark structure: the four QA task types (MC, T/F, RSW, NSW) span regional to national granularity and different reasoning demands, and the prompt templates in the appendix support reproducibility and reuse.

Honest and reasonably thorough ablation study (Table 3): each of the three modules is evaluated individually and in combination, showing complementary gains (e.g., T/F 58.47→79.21 with full combination), which supports the architectural claims beyond a single headline number.

Interpretability analyses add scientific value: the pressure-level weight analysis (humidity peak at 950 hPa, temperature at 100 hPa in appendix Fig. 8) and temporal weighting of red vs. blue warnings (Fig. 6, appendix Fig. 9) are consistent with known meteorological physics, lending credibility that the modules learn meaningful structure rather than artifacts.
Good reproducibility practices: full training/evaluation hyperparameters (appendix Table 3), GPT-4o scoring rubric (appendix Fig. 7), and a commitment to releasing code and data.

Motivation is well-articulated: the three challenges (sample scarcity, 3D data-text misalignment, MLLM limitations on 4D data) are clearly connected to the dataset design and the three proposed modules.
weaknesses: The 'prediction' framing overstates operational relevance: inputs are ERA5 reanalysis fields over the 12 hours starting at warning issuance. Reanalysis is produced post hoc and unavailable in real time, so the system as evaluated is a hindcast/nowcast-style classifier, not a deployable early-warning system as claimed in the Introduction. Using forecast fields (or at least discussing this gap) is needed to support the 'AI-driven weather forecasting' claim.

The closed-source comparison is not meaningful: GPT-4o receives four variables compressed into a three-channel u/v wind + precipitation visualization (as in ClimateMate), while the fine-tuned MLLMs ingest the full 185-channel 4D data with task-specific LoRA fine-tuning on in-domain data. The reported '35-60% improvements' (e.g., T/F 0.19 vs. 87.13) largely reflect input format and fine-tuning rather than the proposed architecture; the paper does not disentangle this.

Comparison baselines are narrow and omit directly relevant prior work: no comparison with existing extreme-weather MLLMs such as ExtremeAd (Chen et al. 2024, cited in Related Works), nor with specialized weather/extreme-event models. Given the claim of a 'first' MLLM for raw meteorological data, a head-to-head with the closest prior system is warranted.

The three modules are technically modest: DTGF is a standard temporal gating on adjacent-frame differences (Eq. 1-3), TGCA is essentially channel cross-attention with text (Eq. 7-9), and TGS is a Gaussian spatial mask from text coordinates (Eq. 4-6). Each is a reasonable engineering choice, but the novelty is incremental; the dataset, not the architecture, is the primary contribution.

NSW task performance is near-chance (2.1/5 best model, and only 651 samples at 0.4% of the data), suggesting the task is either ill-posed or insufficiently resourced; more analysis of failure modes is needed before presenting it as a benchmark capability.
NSW scoring relies on GPT-4o with an open-ended rubric, introducing evaluator subjectivity; no human-annotator agreement or deterministic metric is reported for this task.

Potential shortcut-learning risk is not addressed: CMA warning texts follow templates with geographic and seasonal regularities; the paper does not report controls (e.g., text-only or shuffled-data baselines) demonstrating the model actually uses the 4D meteorological fields rather than priors in the prompt.

Presentation issues: several typos ('MLLMsfrom', 'threshed'), an inconsistency between Fig. 4 legend (NSW 0.4%) and surrounding text, and the naming convention (RSW vs. Region-SW) is used inconsistently. These are correctable but detract from clarity.

strengths: The MP-Bench dataset is a substantial and novel contribution: 421,363 pairs of raw multi-year ERA5 fields with severe weather warnings, seven warning types, four QA task formats spanning regional to national granularity, and a temporally clean year-wise (2023/2024) split. Table 1 shows no existing benchmark jointly offers large-scale text events, multiple severe weather types, and fine (1h) temporal alignment.

The proposed modules (DTGF, TGS, TGCA) are well-motivated and target the specific structure of 4D meteorological data (temporal, spatial, vertical pressure dimensions), and the design avoids the lossy flattening of 4D fields into RGB images used by prior MLLM approaches.

The evaluation is reasonably broad: four open-source MLLM backbones plus GPT-4o, four task types with accuracy and Macro-F1, module-level ablations, temporal-window-length ablations (1h/6h/12h), and a cross-regional generalization test on NOAA Storm Events data.

The supplementary analysis linking learned module weights to physically meaningful patterns (e.g., 500 hPa meridional wind, CMA warning criteria for snowstorm/gale/hail timing) adds credibility and interpretability to the learned attention mechanisms.
weaknesses: Task framing undermines the 'prediction' claim: warnings issued at time t are paired with ERA5 fields spanning [t, t+11], i.e., the model observes reanalysis data covering the very period the warning describes. ERA5 is a reanalysis (assimilated observations), not an operational forecast input, so this is closer to reanalysis-based diagnosis/nowcasting than to end-to-end forecasting. The paper does not discuss this distinction or its implications for operational relevance.

The Baseline vs. MMLM comparison in Table 2 confounds two changes: the number of pressure levels (3 vs. 185 channels) and the three proposed modules. The observed gains therefore cannot be attributed cleanly to the modules. The ablation (Table 3) partially addresses this but is run on only a 5,000-sample subset, and its full-configuration numbers (e.g., MC-main 58.27) are far below the headline Table 2 result (72.37), leaving the headline gains insufficiently decomposed.

Ablation evidence for the modules is mixed: in Table 3, TGS alone degrades T/F (54.81 vs. 58.47), several two-module combinations underperform single modules (e.g., DTGF+TGS drops T/F to 56.63 vs. DTGF alone 53.28/57.23), and the '19.36% overall gain in MC-sub' is measured against an inconsistent reference point. The claimed complementary synergy is not consistently supported.

The GPT-4o results (T/F accuracy of 0.19%, below random guessing) strongly suggest an evaluation-harness or prompt-formatting problem rather than a genuine model capability, which weakens the closed-source comparison and the framing that it 'establishes the critical necessity of the proposed MMLM'.

The NSW task's LLM-as-a-judge scoring (best score 2.1/5) is coarse, and self-evaluation biases of GPT-4o as judge (which the paper itself cites in [29]) are not mitigated by human verification on a sample of outputs.

The dataset covers only two years (2023–2024), a single country, and 0.25° resolution; the authors themselves concede hail detection suffers at this resolution. Long-term inter-annual variability and rare-event coverage (hail, snowstorm < 4%) remain unaddressed.

There is no non-MLLM baseline (e.g., a CNN/ViT classifier or standard nowcasting model) on the MC/T/F tasks, so it is unclear how much of the difficulty is inherent to the data versus the MLLM paradigm, and no comparison against any prior severe-weather prediction method.

Several presentation issues reduce clarity: Table 3 vs. Table 2 inconsistencies are not clearly explained in the main text; the text oscillates between 37, 185, and 3 channel descriptions; typos ('cores of 1 and 0'); and the description of how TGS/TGCA obtain text-event coordinates at inference time (vs. potential label leakage from warning text) is not fully specified.

strengths: MP-Bench is a genuinely new and sizable resource: 421,363 multimodal pairs pairing ERA5 4D fields (5 variables x 37 pressure levels, 12h window at hourly resolution) with official CMA severe weather warnings, covering 7 event types, with a year-wise train/test split (2023/2024) and a cross-regional NOAA subset for generalization testing. This addresses a real gap identified in Table 1 (existing datasets either lack gridded meteorology or lack text warnings).

The three proposed modules (DTGF, TGS, TGCA) are simple, well-motivated, and each targets a distinct dimension (temporal, spatial, vertical) of 4D meteorological data; the ablation in Table 3 isolates individual and combined contributions under identical 185-channel inputs, showing consistent gains (e.g., MC-main 42.73 -> 58.27).

Supplementary analysis connecting learned attention to physically meaningful patterns (500 hPa wind for gales, 850-875 hPa for low-level moisture, DTGF temporal weight differences matching CMA warning issuance criteria for snowstorm/gale/hail) adds credibility beyond raw accuracy numbers.

Broad experimental coverage: 4 base MLLMs, comparison to a closed-source model (GPT-4o), temporal-window ablation (1h/6h/12h), cross-geographical evaluation, and a case study of misclassified samples.
Reproducibility intent is stated (code and dataset to be released) and training/evaluation hyperparameters are fully documented in Tables 8-9.
weaknesses: Fundamental practical validity concern: the pipeline ingests ERA5 reanalysis data, which is produced retrospectively and is not available in real time. The paper motivates the work as an operational, end-to-end early-warning system, but forecasting warnings from reanalysis fields is not the same task as forecasting from real-time NWP output. This undermines the claimed application scenario and should at minimum be discussed; no experiment uses genuinely forecast-available inputs.

The headline baseline comparison (Table 2) is confounded: baselines are fine-tuned on 3-channel compressed inputs while MMLM uses 185 pressure-level channels with the new modules. The huge gaps (e.g., Macro-F1 26.88 -> 50.88) therefore mix the effect of richer input representation with the effect of the proposed modules; a baseline fine-tuned on the full 185-channel representation without the modules is needed to attribute the improvement fairly.

Absolute performance on the most practically relevant task (NSW, generating nationwide warnings) is very weak: the best model scores 2.1 on a 0-100 scale, and the NSW evaluation relies on GPT-4o LLM-as-judge, which is noisy and has known self-preference biases; no human validation of the judge's scores against meteorological experts is reported.

The dataset spans only two years (2023-2024) of warnings for a single country, which is short for learning inter-annual meteorological variability and raises questions about the 'multi-year' framing; the class imbalance mitigation (49,660 sampled 'normal' entries) is described but its sensitivity is not analyzed.

Technical presentation of the modules has gaps: the dimensionality in Eq. (1) (Delta x_t in R^{B x 1 x L x C} from an L2 norm 'in channel dimension') is confusingly stated; how the learnable 3D convolution fusion layer and sigma/alpha in TGS are set or learned is not specified in the main text.

Missing comparisons to relevant non-MLLM baselines: no evaluation against specialized severe-weather prediction methods (e.g., models on SEVIR/GridRad-Serve) or even simple climatology/persistence baselines, so it is impossible to judge whether the MLLM approach adds value over conventional means for the underlying prediction task.

Cross-regional generalization is tested on only 1,000 NOAA samples with a large accuracy drop (to 64.2%), and the mapping of US categorical event types onto CMA-style type/level taxonomies is described only briefly, leaving validity of this transfer evaluation uncertain.

Writing quality issues: typos ('Meteorolo gical'), a broken table reference ('(As shown in Tab. )'), and claims of being 'the first' to use MLLMs on raw meteorological data that are somewhat overstated given cited prior multimodal benchmarks.

strengths: MP-Bench is a genuinely new resource: 421,363 aligned pairs of raw ERA5 4D meteorological fields (5 variables x 37 pressure levels, 12h window at 1h intervals) with official CMA severe weather warnings, covering 7 event types with nationwide, year-round coverage. The comparison in Table 1 shows no existing dataset provides this combination of scale, raw reanalysis data, and 12h (1h-interval) temporal alignment.

The paper targets a real and clearly articulated gap: existing pipelines compress high-dimensional meteorological data into daily averages or few-channel RGB-like inputs, discarding vertical structure and temporal dynamics. Directly ingesting 4D gridded data into an MLLM is a reasonable and well-motivated direction.

The three plug-and-play modules (DTGF temporal gating, TGS text-driven Gaussian spatial masking, TGCA text-driven channel attention) are sensible, lightweight, and well-motivated by the structure of 4D meteorological data (temporal, spatial, vertical dimensions).

The experimental protocol is relatively thorough: four base MLLMs, comparisons against closed-source GPT-4o and fine-tuned 3-channel baselines, ablations of each module individually and in combination, temporal-window-length analysis (Table 4), and a cross-geographical generalization test on NOAA Storm Events data (Sec. 5.4.3).

The appendix provides physically meaningful sanity checks: DTGF temporal weight differences align with CMA warning issuance criteria (e.g., snowstorm and hail timing patterns), and TGCA channel weights concentrate on meteorologically meaningful pressure levels (500 hPa winds, 950 hPa winds, 300 hPa temperature). Training/evaluation hyperparameters are documented in detail (Tables 8-9), supporting reproducibility once data/code are released.
weaknesses: Absolute performance is weak across the board, which undercuts the practical claims. The best NSW score is 2.1 on a 0-100 scale (essentially failure), MC-sub Macro-F1 peaks at 29.31, and RSW accuracy reaches only 71.23. The paper frames gains over baselines as evidence of success, but a 2.1/100 on the headline generation task suggests the model cannot yet perform the envisioned end-to-end warning pipeline. The claim of 'strong performance across multiple tasks' in the abstract overstates the results.

There is an apparent numerical inconsistency between Table 2 and Table 3: the full MMLM (Qwen2.5-VL) reports MC-main Acc 72.37 in Table 2 but 58.27 in the ablation (Table 3), and the text claims a '19.36% overall gain' while Table 3 shows 42.73 to 58.27 (15.5 points). The 5,000-sample ablation subset presumably explains part of this, but the discrepancy is not reconciled and weakens confidence in the reported numbers.

The headline comparison in Table 2 confounds two factors: the baseline is fine-tuned on 3-channel meteorological inputs while MMLM uses 185 channels plus the three modules. The gain attributed to the modules is therefore partly attributable to richer input data. The ablation (Table 3) mitigates but does not fully resolve this, since it is run on a 5,000-sample subset with lower absolute numbers than the main results.

NSW evaluation relies on GPT-4o as an LLM-as-a-judge with a self-designed rubric. Prior work (and ref [29] cited by the authors themselves) documents LLM-judge self-preference bias, and no human-expert validation of the rubric or agreement statistics (e.g., correlation with human meteorologist scores) is reported. Given NSW is the flagship 'end-to-end warning generation' task, the 2.1 score's meaning is uncertain.

Potential shortcut-learning concerns are not addressed. ERA5 reanalysis is used at warning-issuance time; warnings are issued by forecasters based on observed weather that is substantially present in contemporaneous reanalysis fields. Tasks like T/F may be solvable largely from current conditions rather than genuine forward prediction. The authors do not report any analysis isolating whether the model learns forecast-relevant dynamics versus contemporaneous correlations.

Scope limitations are acknowledged but constrain significance: only China-region data, only 2 years (2023 train / 2024 test), 5 variables, and template-like warning text. The cross-region test is only 1,000 NOAA samples with mismatched category taxonomies. Severe class imbalance persists (gale 43.5%, snow storm 1.5-1.7%), and the paper notes rare types remain difficult.

Novelty of the technical contribution is modest: temporal gating, Gaussian spatial masks, and text-conditioned channel attention are each straightforward combinations of standard components. The dataset is the primary contribution; the modeling contribution is incremental.

Reproducibility is promised ('source code and dataset will be made publicly available') but nothing is released at submission time, and the CMA warning data's licensing/redistribution terms are not discussed, which matters for a dataset paper.

Presentation issues: some qualitative claims (e.g., Figure 4 weight-difference interpretations, the CoE contour analysis in the case study with only 20 samples) are post-hoc and anecdotal rather than statistically supported; minor inconsistencies (gain percentages, Figure 3 percentages summing oddly, 371,703 cleaned + 49,660 negatives = 421,363 stated as 'warning pairs') require careful checking.
